>[!note] Gamma and Theta
>**Gamma** and **theta** are two of the [[2.3.4 Greeks|Greeks]], the sensitivities of an option's value $f(S, t)$ to its inputs. Gamma is the second derivative of the value with respect to the stock price $S$. It measures how fast [[2.3.4a Delta|delta]] changes as $S$ moves, and it is the convexity (curvature) of the value in $S$. Theta is the derivative of the value with respect to calendar time $t$, with $S$ held fixed. It measures **time decay**, the change in value as time passes and the stock stays where it is. The two definitions are
>$$\Gamma = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2} = \frac{\partial \Delta}{\partial S}, \qquad \Theta = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}.$$
>Gamma is the change in delta per $\$1$ move in the stock. Theta is in dollars per year, so one calendar day changes the value by about $\Theta/365$.
>
>For European options on a stock with continuous dividend yield $q$, the [[2.3.3f Black-Scholes-Merton Formula|Black-Scholes-Merton formula]] gives closed forms. Let $K$ be the strike, $r$ the continuously compounded risk-free rate, $\sigma$ the volatility, and $\tau = T - t$ the time to expiry. Let $N$ be the standard normal CDF and $n(x) = e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ its density. With
>$$d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r - q + \sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{\tau},$$
>a call and a put with the same strike and expiry have the same gamma,
>$$\Gamma = \frac{e^{-q\tau}\,n(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt{\tau}} > 0.$$
>A long option always has positive gamma. Theta differs between the call and the put:
>$$\Theta_{\text{call}} = -\frac{\sigma S e^{-q\tau}\,n(d_1)}{2\sqrt{\tau}} + qSe^{-q\tau}N(d_1) - rKe^{-r\tau}N(d_2),$$
>$$\Theta_{\text{put}} = -\frac{\sigma S e^{-q\tau}\,n(d_1)}{2\sqrt{\tau}} - qSe^{-q\tau}N(-d_1) + rKe^{-r\tau}N(-d_2).$$
>Each theta has three terms with separate causes.
>- The first term is the same for both options and is always negative. It is the value lost because the stock has less time left to move, and it is largest near the strike.
>- The middle term comes from dividends. As expiry nears, fewer dividends remain to be paid before $T$, so the call gains and the put loses.
>- The last term comes from the strike. As expiry nears, the present value of $K$ rises toward $K$. The call holder pays $K$ and loses, and the put holder receives $K$ and gains.
>
>The [[2.3.3e Black-Scholes-Merton Equation|Black-Scholes-Merton equation]] ties gamma to theta. For a position that is delta neutral ($\Delta = 0$) and has value $\Pi$, the relation among the Greeks reduces to
>$$\Theta + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\,\Gamma = r\Pi.$$
>So a delta-neutral position with a large positive gamma has a large negative theta, and the reverse. Over one short period $dt$, a delta-hedged long option, with its hedge financed at $r$, earns approximately
>$$\text{P\&L} \approx \frac{1}{2}\Gamma\left[(dS)^2 - \sigma^2 S^2\,dt\right].$$
>The hedge breaks even when the stock moves by $|dS| = \sigma S\sqrt{dt}$, whatever the size of gamma.
>- A **long gamma** position is, for example, a bought and delta-hedged option. It gains on days when the stock moves more than this and loses on quieter days.
>- A **short gamma** position is, for example, a written and delta-hedged option. It earns the time decay on quiet days and loses on days with large moves.
>
>The formulas assume the Black-Scholes-Merton setting: a frictionless market, geometric Brownian motion with constant $\sigma$, and constant $r$ and $q$. [[2.3.4a Delta]] covers the first-order sensitivity to $S$, and [[2.3.4c Vega and Rho]] covers the sensitivities to $\sigma$ and $r$.

# Intuition

A delta hedge matches the option's slope at today's stock price. The option's value curve bends, so the hedge is exact only for very small moves. Gamma measures the bend. The bend has value for the option holder. After a delta hedge, a large move in either direction leaves the holder with a gain. Theta is what the holder pays for this. A hedged holder loses a little value on each day the stock stays still. In the Black-Scholes-Merton price, the gains and the losses cancel on average when the stock moves with volatility $\sigma$.

The figure shows the gamma of a call with $K = 100$, $\sigma = 30\%$, $r = 5\%$, $q = 2\%$ and expiry $T = 1$. The stock price $S$ runs to the right, and calendar time $t$ runs into the page from $0$ to $0.96$. The red line marks $S = K$. With one year left, gamma is a low, wide hump with a peak of $0.0147$ near $S = 85$. With $0.04$ years left, the hump is narrow and peaks at $0.0668$ near the strike. Gamma away from the strike falls toward zero. At expiry the payoff is a straight line on each side of $K$, so all of its curvature sits at the kink.

# Properties

#### *(Where Gamma Is Large)* Gamma is largest near the money and close to expiry, and it depends on $\sigma$ and $\tau$ mostly through $\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$.

At the money ($S = K$) with a short time to expiry, $d_1$ is close to $0$ and $n(d_1) \approx 1/\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 0.4$. Gamma is then about
$$\Gamma \approx \frac{0.4\,e^{-q\tau}}{S\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}.$$
This grows without limit as $\tau \to 0$. Away from the money, $|\ln(S/K)|$ becomes large compared with $\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$, so $n(d_1)$ and gamma go to zero. The hump has a width of about $\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$ in log price. When $\ln(S/K)$ moves by $\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$, $d_1$ moves by $1$, and $n(d_1)$ falls to about $61\%$ of its peak. The exact peak in $S$ sits where $d_1 = -\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$, which is below the strike. For the one-year call in the figure above, it is at $S = 85$. Raising $\sigma$ has the same effect as adding time. It lowers gamma at the money and raises it far from the money.

#### *(Reading Theta Across Stock Prices)* Theta is most negative near the strike, and a deep in-the-money European put can have positive theta.

The figure uses $K = 100$, $\sigma = 25\%$, $r = 5\%$, and $q = 2\%$. Far from the strike, $n(d_1) \approx 0$, so only the dividend and strike terms remain. A deep out-of-the-money option has theta near zero, since it has little value left to lose. A deep in-the-money call has $N(d_1) \approx N(d_2) \approx 1$, so its theta tends to $qSe^{-q\tau} - rKe^{-r\tau}$, which is $-1.75$ per year at $S = 160$. A deep in-the-money put tends to $rKe^{-r\tau} - qSe^{-q\tau}$, which is $+4.14$ at $S = 40$. Such a put is worth less than its payoff $K - S$, because the holder waits until $T$ for the strike. As the wait shrinks, the put's value rises toward the payoff. Differentiating [[2.3.1d Put-Call Parity|put-call parity]] in $t$ gives
$$\Theta_{\text{call}} - \Theta_{\text{put}} = qSe^{-q\tau} - rKe^{-r\tau}.$$
So the call and put curves at the same maturity differ by a straight line in $S$. With three months left, the call's theta reaches its minimum of $-11.28$ per year near the strike. With one year left, the trough is shallower and wider.

>[!warning] Sign of the Strike Term in the Put Theta
>The Module 8 notes print the last term of the put theta as $-rKe^{-r\tau}N(-d_2)$. The correct sign is $+$, as the derivation below and the parity relation above show. The plots of put theta in the same notes are positive for deep in-the-money puts, which matches the correct sign.

#### *(Delta Hedging in Practice)* Real hedges are dynamic, discrete, and sometimes biased, and their cost grows with gamma.

A hedge is dynamic because delta changes whenever $S$ or $t$ changes, so the desk resets the share count again and again. It is discrete because the desk trades at intervals, for example once a day, and not continuously. Between two trades the position carries the unhedged gain or loss $\frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2$. A book with high gamma therefore needs more frequent trades to stay close to neutral. A hedge can also be biased, meaning that the desk holds more or fewer shares than $\Delta$ on purpose. It may do so to save trading costs or to keep some exposure to the stock's direction. The right schedule depends on frictions, such as transaction costs and the cost of borrowing shares to sell short. It also depends on the nature of the position, for example its size and how long the desk will hold it. [[2.3.3d Delta Hedging]] shows the same rebalancing on a binomial tree.

#### *(Monetizing Convexity)* A hedged long-gamma position makes money only when the stock moves more than the volatility built into the option's price.

Each rebalance of a long-gamma hedge sells shares after a rise and buys after a fall. Over a day the position gains $\frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2$ and pays $\frac{1}{2}\Gamma\sigma^2S^2\,dt$ in time decay and financing. A trader who wants to earn from the moves wants high gamma, but not too close to expiry. Near expiry, gamma sits in a narrow band around $K$. One large move takes the stock out of the band, and the gamma is gone. Meanwhile the daily theta is at its largest. The trader sets up the position by buying options whose volatility input is low compared with the moves the trader expects. Traders call this buying cheap volatility. [[2.3.5a Implied Volatility]] explains how the market's $\sigma$ is read from prices, and [[2.3.5c Volatility Trading]] computes the profit of this trade.

#### *(Hedging Flows Move the Stock)* Long-gamma hedgers trade against the stock's moves and damp its volatility, while short-gamma hedgers trade with the moves and amplify it.

A hedger who owns options holds $-\Delta$ shares per option. After a rise, delta goes up by about $\Gamma\,dS$, so the hedger sells about $\Gamma\,dS$ more shares into the rise. After a fall, the hedger buys. These trades push the price back and reduce the stock's volatility. A hedger who has written options holds $+\Delta$ shares and does the opposite. That hedger buys after a rise and sells after a fall, which pushes the price further and raises volatility. Each $\$1$ move calls for a trade of $\Gamma$ shares per option. So large positions near the money and close to expiry produce the largest trades.

A convertible bond is a bond that the holder may exchange for a fixed number of the company's shares. It therefore contains a call option on the stock. Suppose a company has a large amount of convertible bonds outstanding and hedge funds hold much of it. The funds hedge by selling the stock short, and they are long gamma. Their rebalancing sells the stock on rises and buys on falls, which damps the stock's volatility.

# Derivation

The first part derives the formulas for gamma and theta. The second derives the one-day profit and loss of a hedged option, which is the trade-off in the callout.

>[!example]- Proof of the gamma and theta formulas
>Start from the call price $c = Se^{-q\tau}N(d_1) - Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$ and the call delta $\Delta = e^{-q\tau}N(d_1)$ ([[2.3.4a Delta]]). Two facts shorten the algebra. First, $d_1$ and $d_2$ differ by $\sigma\sqrt{\tau}$, which does not depend on $S$, so both have $\partial d_i/\partial S = 1/(S\sigma\sqrt{\tau})$. Second, the two densities satisfy
>$$Se^{-q\tau}\,n(d_1) = Ke^{-r\tau}\,n(d_2).$$
>To check it, note that $n(d_2)/n(d_1) = e^{(d_1^2 - d_2^2)/2}$ and $(d_1^2 - d_2^2)/2 = \sigma\sqrt{\tau}\,d_1 - \sigma^2\tau/2 = \ln(S/K) + (r - q)\tau$.
>
>For gamma, differentiate the delta in $S$ by the chain rule:
>$$\Gamma = e^{-q\tau}\,n(d_1)\,\frac{\partial d_1}{\partial S} = \frac{e^{-q\tau}\,n(d_1)}{S\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}.$$
>The put delta is $-e^{-q\tau}N(-d_1) = e^{-q\tau}[N(d_1) - 1]$, which differs from the call delta by a term without $S$. So the put has the same gamma.
>
>For theta, differentiate $c$ in $t$, using $\partial \tau/\partial t = -1$. The factor $e^{-q\tau}$ gives $+qSe^{-q\tau}N(d_1)$, and the factor $e^{-r\tau}$ gives $-rKe^{-r\tau}N(d_2)$. The two density terms are $Se^{-q\tau}n(d_1)\,\partial d_1/\partial t - Ke^{-r\tau}n(d_2)\,\partial d_2/\partial t$. By the identity they combine into $Se^{-q\tau}n(d_1)\,\partial(d_1 - d_2)/\partial t$. Since $d_1 - d_2 = \sigma\sqrt{T - t}$, this derivative is $-\sigma/(2\sqrt{\tau})$, which gives the first term of $\Theta_{\text{call}}$.
>
>For the put, differentiate parity, $c - p = Se^{-q\tau} - Ke^{-r\tau}$, in $t$. This gives $\Theta_{\text{call}} - \Theta_{\text{put}} = qSe^{-q\tau} - rKe^{-r\tau}$. Solve for $\Theta_{\text{put}}$ and use $1 - N(d_1) = N(-d_1)$ and $1 - N(d_2) = N(-d_2)$. The result is the put formula in the callout.

We now derive the one-day profit and loss (P&L) of a delta-hedged long option. Hold one option, sell $\Delta$ shares short, and borrow or lend the net cost $f - \Delta S$ at rate $r$. Over a short period $dt$, the option changes by $df$ and the short shares lose $\Delta\,dS$. The short seller also pays the dividends $q\Delta S\,dt$, and the net cost accrues interest $r(f - \Delta S)\,dt$. The total is
$$\text{P\&L} = df - \Delta\,dS - q\Delta S\,dt - r(f - \Delta S)\,dt.$$
A second-order Taylor expansion of $f$ in $S$ and $t$ gives $df \approx \Theta\,dt + \Delta\,dS + \frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2$. The two $\Delta\,dS$ terms cancel, which is the point of the hedge. What remains is
$$\text{P\&L} \approx \frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2 + \big[\Theta + (r - q)S\Delta - rf\big]\,dt.$$
The first term is the gain from convexity, and the bracket is the cost of carrying the position for $dt$. The relation among the Greeks in [[2.3.4 Greeks]] says the bracket equals $-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$. Substituting gives the formula in the callout. Setting it to zero gives the break-even move $|dS| = \sigma S\sqrt{dt}$. When $r = q = 0$, the bracket is $\Theta$ alone, and the P&L is $\frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2 + \Theta\,dt$. That is a parabola in $dS$ shifted down by one day of time decay.


The animation plots this P&L for $100$ at-the-money calls with $S = K = 100$, $\sigma = 25\%$, $r = q = 0$, and $dt = 1/365$. Each frame has less time to expiry. Gamma grows from $0.0158$ to $0.0798$, and one day of theta grows from $\$1.36$ to $\$6.83$. The parabola gets steeper and its bottom gets deeper. It still crosses zero at the same two points, $\pm\$1.31$. A larger gamma raises the amount at stake each day, but the break-even move depends on $\sigma$ alone. [[2.3.5c Volatility Trading]] extends this P&L to a stock whose realized volatility differs from the $\sigma$ in the price.

# Examples

>[!example] (Easy) Gamma and Theta of a Call Near the Money
>A stock trades at $\$64$ and pays a continuous dividend yield of $1.5\%$. A three-month European call has strike $\$65$. The volatility is $28\%$ per year, and the risk-free rate is $4.5\%$ per year with continuous compounding.
>
>>[!example]- Find the call's gamma and theta, the value it loses in one day if the stock does not move, and its delta after a $\$1$ rise.
>>Here $\tau = 0.25$. The pieces of $d_1$ are $\ln(64/65) = -0.01550$, $(r - q + \sigma^2/2)\tau = (0.045 - 0.015 + 0.0392)(0.25) = 0.01730$, and $\sigma\sqrt{\tau} = 0.14$. So $d_1 = 0.00180/0.14 = 0.0128$ and $d_2 = -0.1272$. The table values are $n(d_1) = 0.3989$, $N(d_1) = 0.5051$, and $N(d_2) = 0.4494$. The discount factors are $e^{-q\tau} = 0.99626$ and $e^{-r\tau} = 0.98881$.
>>
>>Gamma is
>>$$\Gamma = \frac{0.99626 \times 0.3989}{64 \times 0.14} = \frac{0.3974}{8.96} = 0.0444.$$
>>The three terms of theta are $-0.28 \times 64 \times 0.99626 \times 0.3989/(2 \times 0.5) = -7.122$, then $0.015 \times 64 \times 0.99626 \times 0.5051 = 0.483$, and $-0.045 \times 65 \times 0.98881 \times 0.4494 = -1.300$. They sum to $\Theta = -7.94$ per year. One day costs $7.94/365 = \$0.0217$. Repricing the call with one day less gives a loss of $\$0.0218$.
>>
>>The delta is $e^{-q\tau}N(d_1) = 0.99626 \times 0.5051 = 0.5032$. After a $\$1$ rise it is about $0.5032 + 0.0444 = 0.5476$. The exact delta at $\$65$ is $0.5471$. A desk that has written $100$ of these calls must buy about $4.4$ more shares after the rise.

>[!example] (Medium) A Put That Gains From Time
>A stock trades at $\$38$ and pays no dividends. A nine-month European put has strike $\$50$. The volatility is $22\%$ per year, and the risk-free rate is $5.5\%$ per year with continuous compounding.
>
>>[!example]- Find the put's theta and explain its sign. Then find the theta of the call with the same strike and expiry from put-call parity.
>>Here $\tau = 0.75$ and $q = 0$. The pieces of $d_1$ are $\ln(38/50) = -0.27444$, $(r + \sigma^2/2)\tau = (0.055 + 0.0242)(0.75) = 0.05940$, and $\sigma\sqrt{\tau} = 0.22 \times 0.86603 = 0.19053$. So $d_1 = -1.1287$ and $d_2 = -1.3192$, with $n(d_1) = 0.2110$ and $N(-d_2) = 0.9064$. The discounted strike is $50e^{-0.04125} = \$47.979$. The dividend term is zero, so
>>$$\Theta_{\text{put}} = -\frac{0.22 \times 38 \times 0.2110}{2 \times 0.86603} + 0.055 \times 47.979 \times 0.9064 = -1.018 + 2.392 = +1.37.$$
>>The put gains about $\$1.37$ per year as time passes, or $\$0.11$ over $30$ days.
>>
>>The formula prices the put at $\$10.41$, below its payoff $K - S = \$12$. The holder of a European put cannot exercise now and must wait nine months for the $\$50$. As the wait shrinks, the present value of the strike rises, and the put's value rises toward $\$12$. The volatility term is small here because the put is deep in the money and $n(d_1)$ is small.
>>
>>Parity gives $\Theta_{\text{call}} = \Theta_{\text{put}} + qSe^{-q\tau} - rKe^{-r\tau} = 1.374 + 0 - 0.055 \times 47.979 = 1.374 - 2.639 = -1.27$ per year.

>[!example] (Hard) A Dealer Who Is Short Gamma
>A dealer has written $2{,}000$ European calls on a stock at $\$120$ that pays no dividends. The calls have strike $\$120$ and $30$ days to expiry. The volatility is $30\%$ per year, and the risk-free rate is $4\%$ per year with continuous compounding. The dealer is delta hedged. It holds $2{,}000\Delta$ shares and borrows the difference between their cost and the premium at $r$. One day is $dt = 1/365$.
>
>>[!example]- Find the dealer's P&L on a day when the stock does not move, the break-even move, and the P&L on a day when the stock rises by $\$3.10$. Then find the shares the dealer must buy to rehedge, and explain the effect on the stock.
>>Here $\tau = 30/365 = 0.08219$ and $\sigma\sqrt{\tau} = 0.08601$. So $d_1 = (0.04 + 0.045)(0.08219)/0.08601 = 0.0812$ and $d_2 = -0.0048$. The table values are $N(d_1) = 0.5324$, $N(d_2) = 0.4981$, and $n(d_1) = 0.3976$. The discounted strike is $120e^{-0.04 \times 0.08219} = \$119.606$. The call price is $c = 120 \times 0.5324 - 119.606 \times 0.4981 = \$4.309$, with $\Delta = 0.5324$ and
>>$$\Gamma = \frac{0.3976}{120 \times 0.08601} = 0.03853, \qquad \Theta = -\frac{0.30 \times 120 \times 0.3976}{2 \times 0.28669} - 0.04 \times 119.606 \times 0.4981 = -27.35.$$
>>
>>On a quiet day the dealer, who is short the calls, gains the time decay $2{,}000 \times 27.35/365 = \$149.85$. The loan is $2{,}000 \times (0.5324 \times 120 - 4.309) = \$119{,}150$, and one day of interest costs $\$13.06$. The net gain is $\$136.79$. The formula $2{,}000 \times \frac{1}{2}\Gamma\sigma^2S^2\,dt = 2{,}000 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 0.03853 \times 0.09 \times 14{,}400/365$ gives $\$136.80$, the same up to rounding. The break-even move is $\sigma S\sqrt{dt} = 0.30 \times 120 \times 0.05234 = \$1.88$.
>>
>>On the day of a $\$3.10$ rise, the dealer's P&L is about
>>$$-2{,}000 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 0.03853 \times \left(3.10^2 - 3.551\right) = -\$233.44.$$
>>Here $3.551 = \sigma^2S^2\,dt$. Exact repricing gives a call worth $\$6.066$ with $29$ days left. The dealer loses $2{,}000 \times 1.757 = \$3{,}513.96$ on the calls, gains $2{,}000 \times 0.5324 \times 3.10 = \$3{,}300.69$ on the shares, and pays $\$13.06$ of interest. The total is $-\$226.32$. The approximation is off by about $\$7$ because it drops terms of higher order in $dS$.
>>
>>The new delta is about $0.5324 + 0.03853 \times 3.10 = 0.6518$, so the dealer must buy about $2{,}000 \times 0.03853 \times 3.10 = 239$ shares. The exact new delta, $0.6486$, gives $232$ shares. The dealer buys after a rise. If many dealers are short gamma on the same stock, their purchases push the price further up, which amplifies its volatility.

# See Also

- [[2.3.4a Delta]], the first derivative whose rate of change is gamma.
- [[2.3.4c Vega and Rho]], the sensitivities to $\sigma$ and $r$, where vega shares gamma's density term.
- [[2.3.3e Black-Scholes-Merton Equation]], whose curvature term $\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$ ties gamma to theta.
- [[2.3.3d Delta Hedging]], the hedge on a binomial tree that gamma forces to be rebalanced.
- [[2.3.5c Volatility Trading]], which splits a hedged option's P&L into a gamma part and a vega part.
